---
title: "Connecticut Gubernatorial Vote Transitions, 1851-1857: Testing the Limits of Ecological Inference"
output: html_document
---

The elections of the 1850s were marked by dramatic shifts in party affiliation. Practitioners of the new political history introduced ecological regression as a way to estimate the transitions of voters between parties from one election to the next. Combined with regressions of vote shares by demographic data, the intent was to describe possible reasons for why voters shifted their party allegiances. The historians who championed this approach used the regression method that Leo Goodman first outlined in 1953 (Goodman 1953).

In recent years, more sophisticated ecological inference models have been developed that improve on Goodman's original method, including the multinomial–Dirichlet method developed by Gary King and others (Rosen et al. 2001). Olivia Lau, Ryan T. Moore, and Michael Kellermann created [eiPack](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RN-2007-018/), an R package that implements these methods (Lau, Moore, and Kellermann 2007).

This project uses eiPack to estimate voter transitions in Connecticut gubernatorial elections from 1851 to 1857, a period of significant political upheaval. The [code is on GitHub](https://github.com/philfeller/election-inferences). The results are [presented as a Sankey diagram](sankey.html) showing the estimated transitions of voters between parties from one election to the next, along with tables showing the estimated transition percentages. The estimates are shown for transparency and are best read alongside the uncertainty analysis described below.

This analysis was intended to be part of a paper on Connecticut politics in the 1850s that I presented at the 2026 American Political History Conference and am expanding for possible publication. The paper's final version dropped any mention of ecological inference because the estimates were not reliable enough to support conclusions, which pointed toward the traditional tools of political history as the better way to understand voter behavior.

The estimates are unreliable because significant uncertainty underlies them. To assess model robustness, I ran each transition model ten times with identical parameters but different random starting points. The resulting variation in estimated transitions—presented in [heatmaps](uncertainty.html)—reveals both the inherent difficulty of inferring individual behavior from aggregate data and the specific challenges posed by the chaotic party upheaval of the 1850s.

Part of the analysis in my conference paper considered the effect that ballot-box mechanics played in shaping voter behavior. A chart of [vote correlations](office_correlation.html) between statewide and local offices illustrates the effect and provides a framework to consider how voters interacted with the political operatives who distributed ballots (Bensel 2004).

The need to provide economic opportunities to young men may also have influenced voter behavior, and I present [charts showing the age distributions](age_distribution.html) statewide and in towns with unusually large native-born, young adult male cohorts.

Finally, I [compare my results to those of Lex Renda](renda.html), whose 1991 dissertation on Connecticut politics in the 19th century included estimates of voter transitions using Goodman's ecological regression method (Renda 1991).

For the mathematically curious, I provide a non-technical [explanation of the ecological inference method](model.html) that I used and how I implemented it.

Census data come from the IPUMS project at the University of Minnesota (Ruggles et al. 2024).

Renda, Lex. 1991. "The Polity and the Party System: Connecticut and New Hampshire, 1840–1876." Ph.D. dissertation, University of Virginia.

Rosen, Ori, Wenxin Jiang, Gary King, and Martin A. Tanner. 2001. "Bayesian and Frequentist Inference for Ecological Inference: The R × C Case." *Statistica Neerlandica* 55 (2): 134–56. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9574.00162.
